problem: SFT navigation methods reach higher success rate but generalize poorly, while training-free/agentic methods generalize better but have lower SR. Existing TF methods use a single static decision loop with simplified memory and no error correction.
motivation: Reliable object-goal navigation is a basic bottleneck for embodied agents. The authors observe that TF methods keep the foundation model's generality but lack human-like memory and an independent monitoring/correction mechanism, so they accumulate errors in abnormal situations (stuck, room/floor exhausted).
key_idea: A training-free Memory-Execute-Review framework: hierarchical memory supports a routine coarse-to-fine Execute pipeline, while an independent Review module detects anomalies (stuck, exhausted room/floor) and switches to corrective modes.
insight: The ablation on HM3D_v0.1 shows the gains come mostly from the Review module (jump out of room +2 SR, jump out of floor +4 SR: 60.10 -> 66.30) and from the Execute pipeline (about +2 SR, +2 SPL), with commonsense memory alone giving only a small SPL change. Being training-free, the method benefits directly from a stronger backbone (Qwen3-vl-plus to GPT-5.2: 68.0 to 70.9 SR), and it does not suffer the zero-shot drop that SFT JanusVLN shows (62.6 to 52.0 SR).
method: Hierarchical memory: short-term (current RGB-D and pose), long-term compressed (BEV exploration-area map and exploration-value map fused over time), long-term uncompressed (sliding-window previous image), and commonsense memory (self, goal and environment rules injected into the prompt).

Observation analysis: a VLM agent scores six directions (0-300° at 60° steps) from local view, stitched global panorama and the exploration-area map, outputs reasons, and fuses scores with historical values by Exponential Moving Average; the argmax direction is the coarse choice.
Path planning: a VLM PlanAgent distills the selected image and reasons into concise subgoals, keeping or updating the previous one.

Action selection and stop: depth-based traversable region gives candidate waypoints (farthest point plus angular samples, shrunk inward), annotated on the image; the VLM picks one, converted to polar coordinates. A StopAgent marks the goal location, the agent stops within T_s of it or at T_max=100 steps.

Two-step review: if the images at t and t-1 are highly similar or the position is unchanged for two consecutive steps, the agent is judged stuck; it excludes the previously chosen direction and picks the next-best one (obstacle-skipping mode).

Multi-step review: uses the exploration map to decide when a room is fully explored, then heads to unexplored rooms; when the floor is exhausted or step count reaches T_e, the phase goal switches to find stairs, then reach a new floor, then resume search.

setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D plus pose; six-direction views (real robot: front camera only)
setting.action_space: candidate reachable waypoints on the image converted to polar coordinates (distance/angle)
setting.simulator: Habitat (MP3D, HM3D v0.1/v0.2, HM3D-OVON) plus a real Unitree G1 humanoid

numbers.evidence: Table 4 Performance of MerNav with different foundation models

numbers.eval_set_note: 3000 val episodes; camera pitch fixed at -30°

numbers_note: Split names for val sets are inferred from the paper's 'validation set' descriptions; the paper does not say val-unseen. HM3D_v0.1/v0.2 are mapped to HM3D-ObjNav.
results: MerNav sets the best SR and SPL among training-free and zero-shot methods on all 4 datasets (e.g. HM3D_v0.1 SR 68.0 vs TopoNav 60.1 / SGM 60.2; HM3D_v0.2 74.8 vs WMNav 72.2). On MP3D (50.8) and HM3D_OVON (45.7) it also exceeds SFT methods such as T-Diff (39.6) and Nav-R^2 (44.0), though SPL on OVON (21.8) trails FiLM-Nav (24.4).
limitations: Uses a maximum of 100 steps instead of the official 500 and relies on costly proprietary VLM APIs; main results use Qwen3-vl-plus for cost reasons.
Real-world evaluation is only two qualitative cases on a humanoid with a front camera only, and no quantitative real-world results; SPL remains low on MP3D/OVON.
Only evaluated on object-goal navigation; the claims about VLN in general are not tested, and thresholds and hand-designed heuristics (floor jump, stuck detection) may be scene-specific.
